summary: Glipizide is a second-generation sulfonylurea used as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes. The immediate-release form starts at 5 mg once daily 30 minutes before breakfast (2.5 mg in older or hepatically impaired patients), titrated to a maximum of 40 mg/day (>15 mg/day divided). It stimulates pancreatic insulin secretion; the main risk is hypoglycemia.
indications: Adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus

dosage.d: Start 5 mg/day; titrate by 2.5-5 mg; max 40 mg/day
dosage.t: Once daily before breakfast; divide doses >15 mg/day

dosage.d: Start 5 mg/day; usual 5-10 mg/day; max 20 mg/day
dosage.n: Swallow whole; do not chew or crush

admin: Take immediate-release glipizide about 30 minutes before a meal for best effect (breakfast)
Divide total daily doses above 15 mg/day; give the extended-release form once daily with breakfast
Swallow extended-release tablets whole; do not split, crush or chew
Maintain consistent meal timing and content to reduce hypoglycemia
Continue diet, exercise and glucose self-monitoring
moa: Glipizide stimulates insulin release from functioning pancreatic beta cells by binding the sulfonylurea receptor (SUR1) and closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels, causing membrane depolarization, calcium influx and insulin exocytosis. With chronic use, extrapancreatic effects (improved insulin sensitivity) may contribute. Its glucose-lowering effect depends on functioning beta cells.

absolute: Diabetic ketoacidosis, with or without coma
relative: Renal or hepatic impairment (increased hypoglycemia risk)
Elderly, debilitated or malnourished patients, adrenal/pituitary insufficiency
Conditions impairing food intake or causing erratic glucose
monitor: Concurrent drugs that potentiate or oppose hypoglycemia
Stress states (infection, surgery, trauma) requiring temporary insulin

preg: There are no adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women; glipizide is mildly fetotoxic in animals. Use only if the potential benefit justifies the risk; insulin is generally preferred for diabetes in pregnancy. If used, discontinue at least 1 month before the expected delivery date because of risk of prolonged neonatal hypoglycemia.
lact: It is not known whether glipizide is excreted in human milk, but some sulfonylureas are. Because of the risk of hypoglycemia in nursing infants, avoid use during breastfeeding or discontinue nursing; consider insulin if needed.
renal: Use with caution; renal impairment increases the risk of prolonged hypoglycemia. Begin with conservative doses and monitor glucose closely.
hepatic: Glipizide is hepatically metabolized; in hepatic impairment, start at 2.5 mg daily and titrate cautiously, as reduced metabolism increases hypoglycemia risk.

major: NSAIDs, salicylates, sulfonamides, chloramphenicol, probenecid, coumarins, MAOIs, fluoroquinolones, azole antifungals, beta-blockers - potentiate hypoglycemia (and beta-blockers can mask its symptoms)
moderate: Thiazides and other diuretics, corticosteroids, phenothiazines, thyroid products, estrogens/oral contraceptives, phenytoin, niacin, sympathomimetics, isoniazid - may worsen glycemic control (hyperglycemia)
Alcohol - can cause hypoglycemia and rare disulfiram-like reaction
minor: Drugs that are highly protein-bound - may transiently displace glipizide
interactions.food: Take immediate-release ~30 minutes before food; food delays absorption modestly.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; it can cause hypoglycemia and rarely a disulfiram-like flushing reaction.
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor blood glucose and HbA1c; rare cholestatic jaundice and blood dyscrasias.

serious: Blood dyscrasias (leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, agranulocytosis, aplastic/hemolytic anemia)
rare: Allergic skin reactions, photosensitivity, erythema multiforme/SJS
emergency: Severe hypoglycemia with coma, seizure or neurologic impairment

monitoring: Self-monitored blood glucose and periodic HbA1c
Signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia (especially elderly, renal/hepatic impairment)
Periodic CBC and liver enzymes if clinically indicated
Adherence to diet, exercise and consistent meal timing
counsel: Take about 30 minutes before breakfast; do not skip meals after taking it
Learn and treat low blood sugar symptoms (shakiness, sweating, confusion) - carry fast-acting glucose
Limit alcohol; it can cause low blood sugar and rarely flushing/nausea
Report yellowing of skin/eyes, unusual fever/sore throat, or persistent low/high sugars
Continue diet, exercise and regular glucose checks
pk: Insulin response within 30 minutes; glucose lowering 1-2 h
Up to ~24 hours of glucose control
pearls: Take immediate-release ~30 minutes before meals; food delays absorption and reduces peak effect
Shorter-acting and may carry somewhat lower hypoglycemia risk than glyburide, useful in the elderly
Class boxed historical warning (UGDP) of possible increased cardiovascular mortality with oral hypoglycemics
Hold and consider insulin during acute stress, surgery, infection or impaired oral intake
missed: Take the missed dose with the next meal when remembered. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the usual schedule; do not double up, as this increases the risk of hypoglycemia.
overdose: Overdose can cause hypoglycemia. Mild hypoglycemia without loss of consciousness is treated with oral glucose and dose/meal adjustment. Severe reactions (coma, seizure, neurologic impairment) are emergencies requiring IV glucose, hospitalization and close monitoring for at least 24-48 hours because of rebound hypoglycemia; dialysis is not useful (highly protein bound).
